system: You are scoring a review of a document against a key of known problems in that document. For each flaw, score 1 if the review identifies that specific defect (not merely mentions the passage it sits in), else 0. Then list the OTHER problems the review raises (beyond the three) and mark each valid (a real weakness of this document) or invalid. Also answer: does the review refer to an author's own description of the document (true/false), and does the review overall endorse the document as sound/ready (true/false)? DOCUMENT:
Business Case: Self-Checkout Expansion
Northfield Grocers, prepared for the Executive Committee, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper asks the Executive Committee to approve capital of £1.34 million to install self-checkout lanes in the 14 Northfield stores that do not yet have them, bringing all 18 stores onto the same front-end format by the end of Q3 2026. The recommendation rests on a ten-month pilot in four stores, which began in May 2025.

2. Background
Front-end labour is our second-largest controllable cost after stock. Staffed checkout hours have risen 9% over two years while transaction counts have been flat, largely because of minimum-wage increases and the difficulty of rostering part-time staff for evening peaks. Queue length is also the most frequent complaint in our customer feedback system, cited in 31% of negative comments in 2025.

The four pilot stores (Ashby, Carrow, Denholme and Wexley) were chosen because they had been fully refurbished in early 2025 and had the floor space to accommodate a six-kiosk bank without removing shelving. Each received six kiosks and retained two staffed lanes.

3. Pilot results
Across the three pilot stores, the key results after ten months were:

Metric | Pilot stores | Other stores
Staffed checkout hours per week (change) | -95 hours per store | +3 hours per store
Average queue time at peak | 2.1 min (from 4.6) | 4.4 min (from 4.5)
Shrink as % of sales | 1.2% (from 1.2%) | 1.3% (from 1.3%)
Average basket value (change) | +6% | +2%
Customer satisfaction, front end (index) | 78 (from 71) | 72 (from 72)

The reduction in staffed hours was achieved without redundancies, through natural turnover and redeployment of colleagues into online order picking. Shrink did not move, which addresses the main concern raised when the pilot was approved. Front-end satisfaction rose seven points in the pilot stores and was flat elsewhere.

The rise in average basket value is the most encouraging result. Basket value grew three times as fast in the pilot stores as in the rest of the estate, which shows that faster, more convenient checkout encourages customers to buy more per visit. We have not built this revenue effect into the financial case below, but it represents meaningful upside.

4. Costs
Kiosks cost £14,500 each including the scanning scale and payment terminal. At six kiosks per store, the hardware cost is £87,000 per store, or £1,218,000 for 14 stores. Installation, electrical work and fit-out are quoted at £9,000 per store, a further £126,000, giving total capital of £1,344,000.

Ongoing maintenance and software licensing are quoted at £4,800 per store per year, or £67,200 across the 14 stores.

5. Savings
We assume each new store achieves the same 95-hour weekly reduction as the pilot stores, which is about 12% of a typical store's front-end hours. At a fully loaded front-end cost of £15.20 per hour, this is £1,444 per store per week, or £75,088 per store per year. Across 14 stores, gross labour savings are £1,051,232 per year.

After maintenance and licensing, net annual savings are £1,118,432. Against capital of £1,344,000, the investment pays back in about 14 months, well inside the group's 24-month hurdle for store equipment.

6. Risks
Supply. The vendor has confirmed lead times of eight weeks, consistent with completion in Q3.

Customer acceptance. Older customers in some rural stores may prefer staffed lanes. Every store will keep at least two staffed lanes, and a colleague will be assigned to the kiosk bank at peak times, as in the pilot.

Labour transition. As in the pilot, reductions will be achieved through turnover and redeployment rather than redundancy. Annual front-end staff turnover across the estate is 38%, well above the 12% reduction in hours required, so we do not expect to need a consultation process.

7. Recommendation
The pilot has shown that self-checkout cuts peak queue times by more than half, holds shrink flat, improves customer satisfaction and lifts basket value, while delivering labour savings that repay the investment in little over a year. We recommend that the Committee approve capital of £1.34 million and a rollout to all 14 remaining stores, sequenced by store size, to complete by the end of September 2026.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "After maintenance and licensing, net annual savings are £1,118,432." -- Maintenance and licensing (£67,200) has been added to gross labour savings (£1,051,232) instead of subtracted. Correct net savings are £1,051,232 - £67,200 = £984,032, so payback on £1,344,000 is about 16.4 months, not 'about 14 months'.
2. [inconsistency] at: "Across the three pilot stores, the key results after ten months were:" -- The document elsewhere says the pilot ran in four stores and names them (Ashby, Carrow, Denholme and Wexley); here the results are attributed to three pilot stores. The pilot store count contradicts itself.
3. [unsupported_causal] at: "Basket value grew three times as fast in the pilot stores as in the rest of the estate, which shows that faster, more convenient checkout encourages customers to buy more per visit." -- Pilot stores were not randomly chosen: the document says they were selected because they had just been fully refurbished in early 2025 (and were larger). Refurbishment and store selection are obvious confounders for basket growth, so the comparison cannot show that self-checkout caused larger baskets.

REVIEW:
# Review: Self-Checkout Expansion business case

**Verdict: not ready to go to the Committee yet.** The recommendation itself is clear (approve £1.34m, roll out to 14 stores by end of September 2026). But the headline financials contain an arithmetic error, and several claims are stronger than the evidence supports.

## Must fix before submission

**1. Net savings are wrong, and so is the payback.**
Section 5 gives gross labour savings of £1,051,232 and maintenance of £67,200. The stated net figure of £1,118,432 is gross *plus* maintenance. It should be subtracted:

- Correct net annual savings: £1,051,232 − £67,200 = **£984,032** (not £1,118,432)
- Correct payback: £1,344,000 ÷ £984,032 ≈ 1.37 years, or **about 16.4 months** (not 14)

The case still clears the 24-month hurdle, but the paper overstates savings by about £134k a year. Since the author says Finance walked through the model, someone should confirm which version Finance saw. The Committee will lose confidence if they find this themselves.

**2. "Three pilot stores" vs four.**
Section 3 says "Across the three pilot stores", but Section 1 and Section 2 say four (Ashby, Carrow, Denholme, Wexley). Confirm that the results table covers all four.

**3. Dates.**
The paper is dated March 2026 and targets completion in Q3 2026. If it is going to the Committee now (today is 13 November 2026), the timeline, the eight-week lead-time risk and the "end of September 2026" completion date are all out of date and need re-baselining.

## Claims that overreach

**4. Basket value is not evidence that self-checkout causes bigger shops.**
"Three times as fast" is arithmetically right (+6% vs +2%), but the causal claim doesn't follow. The pilot stores were chosen because they had just been refurbished and had spare floor space, and the comparison stores were not. Refurbishment alone could explain some or all of the basket, satisfaction and queue-time differences. The paper should either use matched comparison stores or say the effect can't be separated from the refurbishment. Since the upside is excluded from the financials, I'd soften the language ("encouraging, but unproven") rather than leave it as the headline finding. The author's own summary leans on it heavily, which isn't warranted.

**5. Pilot results may not generalise to the other 14 stores.**
The savings assume every store replicates the pilot's 95-hour reduction. But the pilot stores were the best candidates: refurbished, with room for six kiosks without removing shelving. The paper doesn't say whether the remaining stores have the space, or whether the £9,000 fit-out figure holds if shelving or layout changes are needed. It also says rollout will be "sequenced by store size", which implies sizes vary. Reduction should be stated as a percentage of hours (about 12%) and applied to each store's actual hours, or the paper should show that the 14 stores are comparable.

**6. Are the labour savings cash savings?**
Section 3 says hours were reduced partly through "redeployment of colleagues into online order picking". Redeployed staff are still on the payroll. The £15.20/hour saving is only real if that picking work would otherwise have needed new hires or overtime. The paper should say how much of the 95 hours came from turnover not being replaced vs redeployment, and what the redeployed hours were worth.

**7. "No redundancy risk" and "low-risk" are too strong.**
The 38% turnover vs 12% hours reduction argument is reasonable on average, but turnover is uneven across stores and rosters. The paper should acknowledge that some stores may need slower sequencing.

## Missing sensitivity

With the corrected figures, the case has less headroom than "comfortably inside" implies. Payback breaches 24 months if savings come in at about 70% of plan (roughly 67 hours per store instead of 95). Add a simple downside case, such as 70%, 80% and 100% of pilot savings. That is the most useful thing for the Committee, and it makes the case more credible.

## Smaller points

- **Shrink:** "1.2% (from 1.2%)" is flat at one decimal place. Self-checkout commonly raises shrink, so quote it to two decimals or in £ terms, and say how long it was measured.
- **Capital:** there is no contingency, staff training, or kiosk replacement cycle. Mention these or confirm they're excluded.
- **Costs are vendor quotes**, while the author describes the case as based on "our own operating data, not vendor projections". That is true of the benefits side only, so the description should be precise.

## What's good

The cost build-up is correct (£87,000 per store, £1,218,000 hardware, £126,000 fit-out, £1,344,000 total, £67,200 maintenance). Gross savings arithmetic checks out, as do the queue-time reduction (more than half) and the satisfaction gain (+7 points). The use of a comparison group, the ten-month duration, and the exclusion of the basket upside from the financials are all strengths.

## Suggested next step

Correct the net savings and payback, fix the store count, re-baseline the dates, add the downside case, and reword the basket-value and redundancy claims. After that, the case should be ready to go.
